cases.obligation: Every provider call is answered exactly once before the projection is handed on.
The prompt tells a change in the tool names it snapshotted, and another run's snapshot of the same roster is the same fact.
A provider request carries the exact generation fields and keeps no state on the wire.
An approval names the tool and the arguments of the one call it settled.
A rule minted from a decision covers what it came from and nothing beside it.
A handle resolves only through the generation that minted it.
A transaction staged from a replaced generation is refused.
An admission is reachable only through the generation that minted it.
Transformed arguments are revalidated before sensitivity or authority is read from them.
A source refresh changes only later admissions, and each generation runs once.
Attaching files to a tool result takes the proof that the call was permitted.
Code outside the crate cannot issue a grant through `Grant::issue`.
Code outside the crate cannot build an approval through `Approved::new`.
Code outside the crate cannot build a `ToolAdmission` from its fields.
Code outside the crate cannot clone an approval to run it a second time.
A run context cannot be descended from outside the crate that mints one.
A run result cannot be invented by a caller that ran no run.
An approved effect journals one stable prepared, started and finished invocation.
The result budget is reserved before a parallel wave is admitted.
Simultaneous preparations cannot oversubscribe the requested ceiling.
A cleanup failure never hides the failure that required the cleanup.
Repeated disposal reuses the first outcome instead of repeating the effects.
Encoded output is bounded after the output guard and before the event.
Nothing a command left running is still running after an early return from it.
An expired rotation is refreshed and written down before it is used.
A refresh cannot move a live credential scope to another account.
A written key appears in no debug output anywhere.
A variable Crucible was started with reaches no command unless the list names it.
An extension's own words cannot be printed as Crucible's.
A path outside the workspace is refused without reading it.
A link retargeted after the verdict leads outside and is refused.
Descriptor descent refuses an intermediate symlink.
A denied program reached through a shell is bounded by confinement instead.
A denied network target is never dialed, and the private proxy is the only route out.
The compatibility matrix is complete and never claims kernel confinement it does not have.
Invocation recovery distinguishes all three crash windows.
Resume refuses an expired approval that has not executed.
Obsolete checkpoint formats are rejected without compatibility aliases.
Resume refuses a live sandbox backend weaker than the one the session recorded.
Every pending outcome survives stop and resume with one provider result.
The shipped agent stands under the definition the wiring asked for.
An agent's instructions reach the definition only through the call that keeps the difference between none and empty.
A window narrowed mid-session redraws what is live at the new width.
Login and model selection keep keys off the screen.
A resumed session redraws the whole conversation and its compaction marker.
Every argument-only invocation answers the same text, on the same stream, with the same exit code.
Every built-in tool advertises the same name, schema text, effect, scheduling and ceilings.
Layered configuration resolves to the same values, and a workspace layer is refused the same widening keys with the same words.
The prompt-cache policy resolves to the same ceiling, the same source per field, and the same refusal when a workspace layer reaches past it.

The installed-extension sweep reads the same manifests in the same order, refuses the same ones with the same words, and refuses a directory over the ceiling whole rather than answering from part of it.

A session writes down the same record of the same turn: the same lines, in the same order, with the same fields — the conversation, the versioned framework companion beside it, and the bounded summaries a continued session reads to rebuild what was sent.

Every provider puts the same bytes on the wire for the same conversation: the same address, the same headers, and a body whose keys, order and shape have not moved. With a cache plan attached it also puts the same marker in the same place, over two turns, and gives the same account of what it encoded.
A printed server record names its environment and shows nothing of what it was set to.
A printed document shows nothing of a variable or a key argument written under a server, as it shows nothing of a variable written at the top.
Code outside the crate cannot build a vendor's provenance for a result except through the bounded constructor, so no restriction sentence or vendor name past its bound reaches a transcript or a log.

Every corpus answer is named once, ends with the line a case waits for, and is reachable under its own name.
A table drawn at 60 columns and narrowed to 30 draws exactly the rows the same answer draws at 30 columns from the start.
In native mode, a table narrowed once the window settles is written again as the rows the same answer draws at the new width from the start.
Every corpus answer resized to each width from 8 to 160 columns, from 160 and from 8, keeps the rows it draws fresh at that width, and none is wider than the width it is folded at.
While a formula is held the window shows the one row `◇ drawing a formula · 2 lines so far` and none of its source, and once it closes that row is gone and the formula is drawn.
In native mode a held formula shows the same one status row and none of its source, and once it closes and is sealed the row is gone and the formula is in the scrollback.
Display math, a mermaid fence and a diff fence each held past its cap are handed on as no block, and what is drawn is exactly the answer as written.
A record filled with tables lets the oldest go with its source before it holds the ceiling's count of them, stays within the ceiling, and charges exactly what each kept line weighs.
Every answer in the cut fixtures, held kinds included, draws the same rows however its text is cut into deltas.
A bullet that wraps continues under the first column of its words.
A numbered item that wraps continues under the first column of its words, at the width of its own number.
A task, done or not, that wraps continues under the first column of its words.
A nested item that wraps hangs under its own words, and not under its parent's.
A quote that wraps shows its bar on every row it takes.
A wrapped item is drawn again under its words, and a wrapped quote with its bar on every row, when the window changes width.
In native mode, a wrapped bullet and numbered item continue under their words, at the width written and after a resize.
In native mode, a wrapped quote shows its bar on every row it takes.
In native mode, a wrapped task, done or not, continues under the first column of its words, at the width written and after a resize.
In native mode, a wrapped nested item hangs under its own words and not its parent's, at the width written and after a resize.
In native mode with the ascii glyphs, a wrapped bullet continues under its words, at the width written and after a resize.
In native mode with the ascii glyphs, a wrapped quote shows its bar on every row it takes, at the width written and after a resize.
The fence is drawn in a frame that names its language.
The ascii frame holds nothing outside the ascii set.
The native screen draws the same frame.
The native screen draws the ascii frame too.
A wrapped code row is marked where it carries on.
The native screen marks a wrapped code row too.
Copying a wrapped code row gives the line as written, with no break where it wrapped.
Copying across two wrapped lines keeps the break the code has between them.
A fence label from the model reaches the terminal as its name and nothing else.
The native screen draws a hostile label as nothing but its name.
A block past its cap is shown as written under a label that says why.
The native screen says why in the label too.
A drag over a whole fenced block copies its code and not the frame's edges.
With the scroll rail drawn, a drag over a whole fenced block copies its code alone.
With the scroll rail drawn, the line after a fenced block follows its code without a gap.
With the scroll rail drawn, a drag from the bottom edge takes the next line alone.
With the scroll rail drawn, a drag that scrolled off the window still copies the code alone.
A blank line of code keeps its place in the frame.
The native screen keeps a blank line of code in its frame.
A label longer than a label may be is cut short with an ellipsis.
The native screen cuts a long label short too.
A held block under its cap carries no refusal.
The native screen gives a held block under its cap no refusal.
A wrapped code row is marked with the glyph of its set, and the ascii set holds no box drawing.
The native screen marks a wrapped code row with the glyph of its set.
An empty fence is its frame and carries no refusal.
The native screen draws an empty fence as its frame.
A drag that touches one row of a drawn table puts the whole source of that table on the clipboard, as it was written.
A drag across two drawn blocks copies both sources, in order with the prose between them.
A drag over a rule copies what is drawn, because a rule has no source apart from its drawing.
The renderer lends every drawn block's source, newest first, under the word the block is drawn as.
A native session keeps and lends the same sources as a fullscreen one.
The Ctrl+O footer counts results among the results and sources among the sources, and keeps its words for results.
The Ctrl+O view stands the sources after the cut results, newest first, each under its word.
A block drawn after the Ctrl+O view opened is not let in under the reader.
A drag over one row of the corpus's drawn table puts the corpus's table source on a real terminal's clipboard, byte for byte, in fullscreen mode.
Ctrl+O on a real terminal in fullscreen mode lists the corpus's tables as they were written, newest first, and steps between them.
Ctrl+O on a real terminal in native mode lists the corpus's tables as they were written, newest first, and leaves no row of the view behind.
a table written without outer bars (a | b over --|--) is drawn as a table in the window: its structure rows are there and the bare delimiter row is not.
In native mode a table written without outer bars is drawn as a table in the scrollback the same way.
A table written without outer bars and then narrowed is the table a window that narrow draws, at the same rows.
In native mode a table written without outer bars and then narrowed is the table a window that narrow draws.
With output.glyphs set to ascii a table written without outer bars is drawn with ASCII structure only.
In native mode output.glyphs ascii gives a table written without outer bars ASCII structure only.
The corpus tables answer draws its table written without outer bars as a table at 40, 80 and 120 columns.
In native mode a table written without outer bars, cut into deltas anywhere including mid-delimiter, draws what the whole answer draws.
A drag over a table written without outer bars copies its source as written and adds no bars.
A delimiter row with another number of cells, a lone row of dashes, and a delimiter-like line in prose leave their lines as prose, exactly as written.
A table written without outer bars is handed on whole as a block with the source it was written as.
A line still arriving is on screen as it comes, whatever it could turn out to be, so a line that is not a table is never held back for one.
In native mode a line still arriving is on screen as it comes, whatever it could turn out to be.
A header stalled part way is drawn as the prose it is until the delimiter row decides, and gives way to the table without leaving a row of itself in the record.
In native mode a header stalled part way never reaches the terminal's scrollback as prose, because a line in doubt is not finished.
A frame drawn between two deltas while a possible header is in doubt, wherever the answer is cut, leaves the screen and the record that drawing the whole answer leaves.
In native mode a frame drawn between two deltas while a possible header is in doubt, wherever the answer is cut, leaves the scrollback that drawing the whole answer leaves.
The reader says a header as prose as it arrives, takes it back exactly once before handing on the table, and never takes back a line that stops looking like a header.
A line that stops looking like a header is never taken back, and is said exactly as written.
A component drawn while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends that line as the prose it was, said once, as if it had never been in doubt.

On a native screen, presenting rows, committing a line or writing a prompt while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was, said once, as if it had never been in doubt.
Committing a line or writing a prompt while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was, said once, as if it had never been in doubt.

A responsive block laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was: the header said once, no blank row added, no table made of it when the delimiter row comes, as for the same words with no header in them.

On a native screen, a responsive block laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars sends it to the scrollback once, as the prose it was, with no table made of it when the delimiter row comes.

A responsive block charged as laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was: the header said once, no blank row added, no table made of it when the delimiter row comes, as for the same words with no header in them.

On a native screen, a responsive block charged as laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars sends it to the scrollback once, as the prose it was, with no table made of it when the delimiter row comes.

An opening laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was: the header said once, no blank row added, no table made of it when the delimiter row comes, as for the same words with no header in them.

On a native screen, an opening laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars sends it to the scrollback once, as the prose it was, with no table made of it when the delimiter row comes.

A divider laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was: the header said once, no blank row added, no table made of it when the delimiter row comes, as for the same words with no header in them.

On a native screen, a divider laid while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars sends it to the scrollback once, as the prose it was, with no table made of it when the delimiter row comes.

Emptying the transcript on a screen while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was and drops it with the rest: no blank row left for it, no table made of it when the delimiter row comes, as for the same words with no header in them.

Emptying a native transcript while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars sends it to the scrollback once, as the prose it was, with no table made of it when the delimiter row comes.

Hanging an answer under a result mark while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars ends it as the prose it was: the header marked and said once, no blank row added, no table made of it when the delimiter row comes, as for the same words with no header in them.

On a native screen, hanging an answer under a result mark while a line may still be the header of a table written without outer bars sends it to the scrollback once, marked, as the prose it was, with no table made of it when the delimiter row comes.
A run whose output is a file is written a table without outer bars as the table, once, and never its header as prose, however the answer is cut into deltas.
A run whose output is a file has not written a line that may still be the header of a table until it is known, and writes it whole when it is not one.
A session replayed onto a recording that stands in for a pipe, wearing a palette, draws a table written without outer bars as the table the screen draws.
The reader says a line is in doubt from its first character until the delimiter row under it is whole, and not for a line that cannot be a header.
Title over =====, and Sub over -----, are drawn as headings and the underline rows are never shown: no row of the window holds ===== or ---, and a rule row is never wider than the words above it.
In native mode the scrollback holds the same: no ===== or --- row, a rule under each of Title and Sub no wider than its words.
A level-1 heading wears a heavy rule (━, ascii =) and a level-2 heading a light one (─, ascii -), each as many columns wide as the words as drawn, whatever the length of the underline written.
The native scrollback wears the same rules, in both glyph sets.
A heading wider than the window wraps, and its single rule is as wide as the last row the words are drawn on; no other row holds a rule glyph.
In native mode a wrapped heading wears one rule as wide as its last row.
A heading already written is laid out again when the window narrows and when the glyph set changes: the rule is as wide as the last row of the words at the new width, in the new set's stroke.
The native scrollback is written again with the heading's rule at the new width and in the new glyph set.

A --- at the start of an answer, after a blank line, or under a list item, a quote, an ATX heading, a closed fence or a closed table is a rule as wide as the window; a === row under a list item or a closed fence is prose, and under an ATX heading is prose beside that heading's own rule.
The native scrollback reads --- and === under what is not a paragraph the same way.
a | b over --|-- with as many cells is a table (a bar is drawn, no bare rule row), never a level-2 heading.
The same in native mode: the bar-less table is still a table.
one cell over --- and a | b over --- over 1 | 2 are level-2 headings with their rules; one cell over :-: stays prose.
The same three answers in native mode.
Title over ===== and Sub over --- with no final line break are headings: the end of the message completes an underline.
The same in native mode, and trailing blanks after the underline are part of it.
Exactly 128 - or 128 = under a short title are headings (levels 2 and 1); 129 - is a full-width rule under prose, and 129 = is prose.
The native scrollback draws a 128-mark underline as a heading and a 129-mark one as it was written, and does the same for a title of 128 bytes against one of 129.

A title of exactly 128 bytes over --- or === is a heading with a rule 128 columns wide; one of 129 bytes over --- stays prose over a full-width rule, and over === stays prose over the row of equals signs.
**  over --- and --  over --- are level-2 headings with a 2-column rule.

An ATX heading with up to three spaces in front of it wears a rule as wide as its words alone: `  # Title` draws `  Title` over a 5-column heavy rule, `   ## Sub` over a 3-column light one, and ascii draws `=`.

In native mode, an ATX heading with up to three spaces in front of it wears a rule as wide as its words alone: `  # Title` draws `  Title` over a 5-column heavy rule, `   ## Sub` over a 3-column light one, and ascii draws `=`.
$5 over --- is a level-2 heading and \*x over === a level-1 heading drawn as *x, since the display-math probe gives up on both.
The same in native mode, and the marker-only titles.
first line, second line over === draws the first line as prose and the second as the heading with its rule.
The same in native mode.
# and a === heading are drawn alike, ## and a --- heading are drawn alike, no # is drawn, and levels 4 to 6 are one row with no rule like level 3.
The same in native mode.
Title over a single = and Sub over a single - are headings with rules of 5 and 3 columns.
The same in native mode.
Three answers holding setext headings (and $5 and \*x titles), each cut into two deltas at every byte, draw the rows the whole answer draws.
The native scrollback of an answer cut into two deltas at every byte equals the one the whole answer keeps.
A title and its underline arriving in separate deltas, however cut, are one heading in the scrollback: the title is written once, with its rule under it.
A title the next line proves prose reaches the scrollback once, as it was written, before that line.

With output redirected and colour on, a title (with markers) over === is written once, as the heading drawn with its rule, only after its underline has arrived: nothing is written before, however the answer is cut; Sub over --- is written the same way.
With output redirected, a title waits for the next line, and when that line is not an underline it is written then as the prose it was.
A drag over a heading copies its words and then its rule as drawn, and Ctrl+O lists no source for it.
The reader says the same blocks for an answer cut into deltas anywhere as for the whole answer.
A paragraph line is in doubt from its first character and after its break, up to the 128-byte cap.
A title opening with $ or a backslash is in doubt from its first character.
A heading block names no source to list.
The heavy rule glyph is one column wide, and differs from the light one in the unicode set only.
The whole-screen window keeps a request to copy to the clipboard as written and refuses a request to read it back.
A picture file or SVG one byte past one mebibyte is refused.
A decoded picture one byte past two mebibytes is refused.
A header that claims four billion pixels is refused, not allocated.
An SVG drawn into more than two mebibytes of pixels is refused.
Only one picture is read or drawn at a time, across threads.
The wait for the decode slot is bounded and ends as OverTime.
The decode slot is released when its holder unwinds.
A PNG payload is refused one byte past one mebibyte.
A Sixel payload is refused wider than six hundred pixels.
The widest, noisiest Sixel payload stays within the size measured for it.
An image in an SVG that is not a data URL is not followed.
The font database holds the one embedded face and nothing from the system.
References that lead back to where they started are refused before the parser follows them.
References that share a target without leading back are drawn.
A picture nested as deep as the parser allows is drawn whatever stack the caller has.
A drawing the renderer panics on is refused, not raised to the caller.
Every file of the hostile corpus is drawn or refused as recorded, and the record and the corpus agree.
No file of the corpus is missing from the record, or the record from the corpus.
Every reference an SVG makes is drawn as if it were not there, and what it names records no open, connect, accept or use.
A resolver planted to use the sentinel changes the output and is found.
A resolver planted to read and discard is found by the pipe that was opened.
A resolver planted to connect is found by the listener that accepted.
The whole corpus drawn in a child process prints nothing.
A diagnostic planted behind an allow is found by the child-process check.
A line planted on the standard output is found by the child-process check.
A panic in the corpus runner is reported as a finding, not lost.
An unbounded loop in the corpus runner is reported as a finding, not waited on.
Generated pictures of every family are decoded, drawn or refused within the ceilings, none panicking or hanging.
A generated case is the same from the same seed and index.
The forged headers of every format are read by the decoder as a size past the ceiling.
A panic planted in the generated runner is reported as a finding.
A loop planted in the generated runner is reported as a finding.
A filter with many named results is refused before it is drawn, whatever the size of the file.
A layer beside the canvas is counted against the two mebibyte ceiling, drawn at it and refused one byte past it.
A small filter and a small layer are drawn.
Filter work is drawn at its ceiling and refused one row past it.
Filter work is added up over the whole drawing, not judged per primitive.
A morphology and a convolution are counted by the window each pixel reads.
A merge is counted by the inputs it draws, and drawn at its ceiling and refused one row past it.
A shape is counted by the pixels it covers inside the canvas, so one far off the page costs nothing.
A stroke and a fill of one path are counted apart.
A corpus file refused for its work is drawn once the work is made small, so the work budget is what refused it.
A dashed stroke is counted by the dashes it is cut into, drawn at the ceiling and refused one dash past it.
A thin dash is counted by the width it is drawn across, and a long one by the pixels it covers.
A dash count no number can hold is refused, and a dash array of zeros is drawn.
A path in a clip is counted by the pixels it fills on the clip's pixmap, drawn at the ceiling and refused one rectangle past it.
Every shape costs its overhead however little it covers, so shapes off the canvas are counted and a few nested uses of them are refused.
A path is counted by the rows each segment crosses: edges along one row are drawn and as many crossing the page are refused.
Edges crowded along a row are counted by the pixels each can walk: tens of thousands across a wide row are refused, and a thousand are drawn.
A dashed stroke of many contours shorter than a pixel is counted by its segments across the rows of the stroke, not only by its few dashes, and refused as the solid stroke is.
A gradient is counted by its stops over the pixels it paints: a thousand stops over a large page are refused, and two are drawn.
The copies nested uses would make are counted and refused before any is made, a use in the definitions among them, and a few levels are drawn.
A copy is counted by the text and attribute bytes it copies: many copies of a long text or path are refused before any is made, and one is drawn.

A gradient costs the pixels it paints and its stops at each together: paints neither of which alone is past the ceiling are refused before they are drawn, and the same paints with two stops are drawn.
A stroke whose edges crowd along a row is counted by the pixels each edge can walk: a wide crowded row is refused before it is drawn, and a narrower one is drawn.
An element outside those drawn is refused wherever it is before the parser sees it, and every element drawn is drawn, as is a name outside them that is only text or an attribute's value.
An SVG inside a filter's image step refuses the picture, and a raster image there is drawn as nothing.
A marker drawn inside a marker is refused before the tree is built, and two markers on one shape, and one on many, are drawn.
A clip or a filter inside a clip is refused before the tree is built, and a clip clipped by another as a whole, and one clip on many shapes, are drawn.
The copies a marker makes at each vertex, a clip sized to each shape it clips, and letters copied where nothing draws them are counted and refused before any is made, and a few of each are drawn.
Each corpus file whose drawing or tree build would take long, by nesting, copies, an element outside those drawn or a gradient's stops, is refused as recorded within the time a refusal may take.
A corpus file refused for an element is drawn once that element is made a group, so the element is what refused it.
A run writing into its root, /tmp and its home together stops at the disk ceiling in total, never at a ceiling per place.
Many small files written into every writable place at once never hold more than the disk ceiling.
Under a disk ceiling /dev and /dev/shm refuse writes, and /dev/null accepts them and holds nothing.
A disk ceiling is refused as unsupported for a run with a writable rule or a writable manifest mount, and taken for a run with neither.
Observing claims no disk ceiling and says a preparation checks --size, while a preparation on the same host takes one.
A run making files until its command time runs out is stopped by that time, and the next run starts with none of them.
Under a disk ceiling every call that sets an extended attribute (setxattr, lsetxattr, fsetxattr, setxattrat) is refused with EPERM, and no attribute value is held.
